name: Time under tension (TUT)

chain: Controlled tempo and pauses extend the time a muscle is loaded
Greater mechanical and metabolic stress per set
More muscle growth across training blocks
angle.text: Lifters use tempo to increase the stimulus from each set and to keep reps controlled, aiming for a bigger, more developed physique. Studies of rep duration give mixed results, and total volume and proximity to failure also shape growth.

lead: Time under tension (TUT) is how long a muscle stays loaded during a set, usually counted as the seconds spent lowering, pausing at the bottom or in a hold, and lifting. Bodybuilders and recreational lifters manipulate it through rep tempo, such as a slow lowering phase or a pause, with the aim of more muscle size and a fuller physique.[1]

The idea comes from the mechanisms usually described for muscle growth: mechanical tension on the muscle fibres, metabolic stress, and muscle damage. Reference sources describe mechanical tension as the leading accepted driver and say that a tempo of roughly 2 to 8 seconds per repetition is commonly considered effective, with load and total volume mattering more over the long term.[2]

Umbrella reviews find resistance training consistently raises muscle mass, with load, weekly frequency and volume among variables with supporting evidence.[3] A study of lifting to failure found muscle fibre activation unaffected by load and repetition duration.[4] A 2023 narrative review of training technique recommended a rep tempo of about 2 to 8 seconds, and a 2022 umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses advised avoiding very slow repetitions of 10 seconds or more.[5][5]
infobox: Seconds of loaded contraction per rep or per set
Eccentric training, pauses, drop sets, low-load training [7][6]

paras: TUT is usually written as a four-number tempo, such as the seconds for lowering, a pause at the stretched position, lifting, and a pause at the top. Increasing any phase lengthens the set, so lifters either use lighter loads for the same repetitions or fewer repetitions with the same weight.[1]

Related ideas include eccentric emphasis, where the lowering phase is slowed because muscles can resist more force when lengthening; pauses to remove rebound; and drop sets and low-load training taken near failure, which extend the loaded time of a set. A 2019 review of eccentric methods suggests tempo eccentric training may suit weaker lifters, to benefit hypertrophy through time under tension.[6]

Muscle growth is described as arising from mechanical tension, which activates mTOR signalling and muscle protein synthesis; metabolic stress, such as lactate and hydrogen ion accumulation and cell swelling; and muscle damage, which correlates poorly with growth and is not considered the main driver.[2] Longer sets raise energy turnover, metabolic stress and ischaemia, and a 2022 review proposed that high TUT, such as slow-tempo and drop-set training, also drives aerobic adaptations including mitochondrial biogenesis and angiogenesis.[7]

A 2006 review in the European Journal of Applied Physiology argued that the usual description of resistance exercise by load, reps, sets and rest is insufficient and proposed additional mechano-biological determinants, including loading time.[8]

The Wikipedia article on muscle hypertrophy summarises two studies often cited in tempo discussions: Burd and colleagues (2012) reported that slow contractions at light loads raised muscle protein synthesis more than fast ones, while Schuenke and colleagues (2012) found that normal-speed training produced greater fibre increases than slow-speed training.[2]

A 14-week study of 10 untrained men, published in PeerJ in 2021, compared 2-second and 6-second repetitions taken to failure on knee extensions; the 6-second condition gave larger isometric strength gains at a 30 degree knee angle, while one-repetition maximum, other joint-angle strength and muscle cross-sectional area did not differ significantly.[5] A 2025 meta-analysis of nine studies (166 participants) on eccentric phase duration found that results for maximal strength and hypertrophy were uncertain, with longer eccentric phases giving similar or greater strength gains in trained participants.[5]

A 2022 umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses (178 primary studies, 4,784 participants) suggested about 10 weekly sets per muscle group, emphasised eccentric contractions, and advised against very slow reps of 10 seconds or more.[5] A 2023 narrative review recommended emphasising long muscle lengths and a tempo of about 2 to 8 seconds, adding that more research is needed on the lengths of the eccentric and concentric phases.[5]

A 2024 umbrella review of 44 reviews found resistance training is a potent stimulus for muscle mass and reported evidence for load, frequency and volume effects.[3] A 2026 American College of Sports Medicine position stand synthesised 137 systematic reviews (over 30,000 participants) and reported that resistance training improved strength, size and power compared with no exercise, that few prescription variables changed primary adaptations, and that heavier loads (80 percent of one-repetition maximum or more) enhanced voluntary strength.[9]

A trial found muscle fibre activation was unaffected by load and repetition duration when sets went to failure.[4] A review proposes high TUT drives aerobic adaptations such as mitochondrial biogenesis.[7] A 2026 randomised trial in runners examined high-TUT strength training and muscular performance.[10]

Lifters typically choose a controlled tempo for isolation work such as curls, leg extensions and lateral raises, and use pauses or slow lowering on exercises where momentum tends to take over. Some programmes label tempo with codes and combine it with progressive overload, tracking load and reps over weeks.[2] Because slower tempos reduce the weight that can be lifted, discussions of TUT commonly weigh it against load and total volume.[3][2]

The usual risks of resistance training apply, including joint and tendon strain from poor form or sudden load increases. Reviews of eccentric methods note the training demands suit lifters differently depending on strength level.[6]

timeline.event: A review in the European Journal of Applied Physiology argues for new mechano-biological determinants of resistance exercise, including loading time.[8]
Burd and colleagues, and Schuenke and colleagues, publish contrasting findings on slow versus normal-speed training.[2]
A Journal of Physiology trial reports fibre activation unaffected by load and repetition duration when sets go to failure.[4]
A PeerJ study compares 2-second and 6-second repetitions to failure over 14 weeks.[5]
A review proposes high TUT as a driver of aerobic adaptations; an umbrella review advises against reps of 10 seconds or more.[7][5]
An umbrella review of 44 reviews examines resistance training variables.[3]
An American College of Sports Medicine position stand synthesises 137 systematic reviews.[9]
